title: Indian Student Abroad Reveals Losing 10 Kilos as Falling Rupee Makes Basic Living Unaffordable
excerpt: A viral blog post captures the hidden cost of the rupee's slide past 90 to the dollar, as Indian students abroad face soaring expenses, top-up loan demands, and deteriorating living conditions.
body:
• An Indian student's blog post about losing 10 kilos due to unaffordable living costs abroad has gone viral, putting a human face on the rupee's depreciation crisis.
  • The rupee has slid past 90 to the US dollar, adding lakhs to the annual cost of overseas degrees and forcing families to take top-up loans.
  • RBI data shows outward remittances for education dropped 23% year-on-year by late 2025, with the decline accelerating into 2026.
  • Demand for top-up education loans from Indian lenders has jumped nearly threefold as loan amounts sanctioned in rupees fall short of fees payable in foreign currency.

An Indian student studying abroad has published a blog post that has struck a nerve across the diaspora, detailing how the falling rupee forced them to lose 10 kilos simply because they could no longer afford adequate meals. The account, reported by NDTV, lays bare the human cost of a currency slide that has turned overseas education from an aspiration into a financial ordeal for middle-class Indian families.

With the dollar now trading above 90 rupees, every monthly remittance from home buys less food, less comfort, and less security. A US university charging $40,000 per year that cost roughly Rs 33 lakh when the rupee was at 83 now costs over Rs 36 lakh at current rates, with no change in the actual tuition, according to Prithvi Exchange managing director Pavan Kavad.

The Numbers Behind the Struggle

The financial strain extends far beyond tuition. Reserve Bank of India data shows outward remittances for education dropped 23% year-on-year by August 2025, with the decline accelerating through the rest of the year. Counselors report that 42% of prospective study-abroad families are now naming alternative, cheaper destinations at their first inquiry, up from 29% in early 2024.

For students already enrolled overseas, the rupee's slide has created a funding gap that existing loan sanctions cannot cover. Mumbai-based education lending platform MPower Financing reports that demand for top-up loans among rupee borrowers has jumped nearly threefold in the past year, with students seeking additional disbursements of Rs 1 to 6 lakh.

"Everything costs more — the course fees, living expenses, even the pocket money. A round-trip ticket that cost around Rs 96,000 a year ago is now close to Rs 1.6 lakh."

— Sunetra Banerjee, parent of a US-based student, as reported by Economic Times

Banerjee told the Economic Times that she and her husband have paid at least Rs 7-8 lakh more than their initial estimates in the first year alone. Her daughter has applied for an additional scholarship; if that falls through, the family will either take a top-up loan or liquidate investments.

The Ripple Effect Across Destinations

The currency crisis is reshaping where Indian students choose to study. Public universities in Germany and Italy, where tuition typically ranges from €3,000 to €4,500 per year, are drawing steady attention. By contrast, high-demand UK programs now tip into the Rs 25-28 lakh range annually once fees and city costs are counted.

According to EduFund, an undergraduate degree from Harvard that cost around Rs 53 lakh in 2021 now translates to nearly Rs 78 lakh. That figure excludes healthcare, visa renewals, and post-study job-search costs, which can add another 10-20% to the final bill.

The US has also seen its F-1 student visa rejection rate climb to a decade-high 44%, while Canada's rejection rate for Indian students has surged to nearly 74%, up from 32% two years earlier, according to Reuters. The combination of higher costs and reduced access is creating a perfect storm for Indian families.

The Emotional Toll

Beyond the financial calculations, the student's blog captures something harder to quantify: the daily erosion of dignity when you cannot afford to eat properly in a foreign country. Students report cutting meals, sharing already cramped accommodation with additional roommates, and working maximum permitted part-time hours while maintaining full course loads.

The viral response suggests the experience is far from isolated. For a generation of Indian families who stretched their finances to give their children an international education, the rupee's slide has turned careful planning into a moving target, with no sign of stabilizing anytime soon.
